lead: Entropy is a property that measures how heat and temperature set the direction of a process. For a reversible path it is defined by dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T. Because the Clausius inequality gives zero around any reversible cycle, the integral between two states is the same for every reversible route. That is why entropy belongs to the state, not the path. Engineers use it on the T-s diagram to see heat as area and to compute ideal-gas entropy changes in compressors, turbines and heat exchangers.
prereq: You need: the Clausius inequality, and ideal-gas processes and specific heats from the first-law topics.

blocks.text: The Clausius inequality says ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 for any cycle; the value is zero for a reversible cycle. Take two reversible paths between state 1 and state 2. Go from 1 to 2 along path A, then return from 2 to 1 along path B reversed. This closed cycle is reversible, so its cyclic integral is zero. Hence the integral of δQ/T from 1 to 2 along A equals the integral along B. The value depends only on the end states. That is the definition of a property.

blocks.where: δQ<sub>rev</sub> is the heat transfer in a reversible process, in kJ; T is absolute temperature, in K; dS is the entropy change, in kJ/K.

blocks.text: S is extensive: 2 kg has twice the entropy of 1 kg at the same state. Specific entropy s = S/m has units kJ/kg·K. For an irreversible process, ΔS is still fixed by the end states; calculate it along any convenient reversible path, not along the real path. The real path gives only ∫δQ/T, which is less than ΔS; the gap is the entropy generated inside the system (see entropy generation).

On a temperature-entropy diagram, plot T in K against s in kJ/kg·K. For a reversible process, δQ<sub>rev</sub> = T dS, so Q<sub>rev</sub> = ∫T dS. The signed area under the path between two entropies is the heat transfer. If T is in K and S in kJ/K, the area is in kJ.

An isothermal reversible process is a horizontal line. A reversible adiabatic (isentropic) process is a vertical line. A Carnot cycle between two temperatures is therefore a rectangle: two horizontal isotherms and two vertical isentropics. The area inside the rectangle is the net work of the cycle; it equals Q<sub>in</sub> − Q<sub>out</sub>.

Slopes. At constant pressure, T ds = dh = cp dT, so dT/ds = T/cp. At constant volume, T ds = du = cv dT, so dT/ds = T/cv. Since c<sub>v</sub> < c<sub>p</sub>, T/c<sub>v</sub> > T/c<sub>p</sub>: through any point the constant-volume line is steeper than the constant-pressure line. The figure draws both for the worked example’s air, from 300 K.

sections.h3: Entropy change of an ideal gas

blocks.text: For an ideal gas with constant specific heats, integrate ds = cv dT/T + R dv/v and ds = cp dT/T − R dp/p. For mass m:

blocks.where: m is the mass in kg; c<sub>v</sub> is the specific heat at constant volume in kJ/kg·K; T<sub>1</sub>, T<sub>2</sub> are absolute temperatures in K; R is the gas constant in kJ/kg·K; v<sub>1</sub>, v<sub>2</sub> are specific volumes in m³/kg; ΔS is in kJ/K.
c<sub>p</sub> is the specific heat at constant pressure in kJ/kg·K; p<sub>1</sub>, p<sub>2</sub> are pressures in the same unit, usually kPa; the other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: Use cp when pressure is held constant and cv when volume is held constant. An isentropic process is reversible and adiabatic; a real adiabatic process has ΔS > 0.

figure.caption: The worked example per kilogram of air. Heating at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K (solid) and the check route, constant volume then isothermal (dashed), end at the same entropy, 0.697 kJ/(kg·K) above the start. The constant-volume line is the steeper one; the shaded area under the solid path is the heat.

spec.aria: Temperature against entropy for air. A solid constant-pressure curve rises from 300 K to 600 K over 0.697 kJ/(kg·K), with the area under it shaded, 301.5 kJ/kg. A steeper dashed constant-volume curve reaches 600 K at 0.498, then a dashed horizontal isotherm reaches the same end point.

examples.question: 2 kg of air is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K. Take cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. Find the entropy change of the air. Check the result by treating the same change as constant-volume heating followed by isothermal expansion.
steps: List the data: m = 2 kg, T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 600 K, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K.
For constant pressure, use ΔS = m c<sub>p</sub> ln(T₂/T₁).
Check. Constant-pressure heating from 300 K to 600 K also doubles the specific volume, so v₂/v₁ = 2.
Constant-volume part: m c<sub>v</sub> ln(T₂/T₁) = 2 × 0.718 × 0.6931 = 0.995 kJ/K.
Isothermal part: m R ln(v₂/v₁) = 2 × 0.287 × 0.6931 = 0.398 kJ/K.
examples.answer: The entropy change is 1.393 kJ/K, positive because heat is added.
examples.check:
import math
m = 2.0
T1 = 300.0
T2 = 600.0
cp = 1.005
cv = 0.718
R = 0.287
ds = m * cp * math.log(T2 / T1)
print(round(ds, 3))

traps: Entropy is a property: ΔS depends only on the end states, so never integrate δQ/T along an irreversible path; use a reversible substitute between the same states.
Put T in kelvin. Using Celsius in ln(T₂/T₁) gives a wrong number and can even make the log invalid.
Use cp for constant pressure and cv for constant volume; they are not interchangeable.
The area under a T-s path is heat only for a reversible path. For an irreversible process it is not the actual heat transfer.
S is extensive (kJ/K); s is per kg (kJ/kg·K). Do not mix them in the same formula.

quiz.q: State the definition of entropy change for a reversible process and give its units.
quiz.a: dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T. S is in kJ/K; specific entropy s is in kJ/kg·K.

quiz.q: Why does the integral of δQ/T define a property even though δQ depends on the path?
quiz.a: For two reversible paths forming a cycle, ∮δQ/T = 0 by the Clausius inequality. So the integrals between the same two states are equal, and the value depends only on the end states.

quiz.q: 1 kg of air is heated at constant volume from 300 K to 600 K. Take cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. Find ΔS.
On a T-s diagram, why is a constant-volume line steeper than a constant-pressure line?
quiz.a: The slopes are dT/ds = T/cv at constant volume and dT/ds = T/cp at constant pressure. Since c<sub>v</sub> < c<sub>p</sub>, T/c<sub>v</sub> > T/c<sub>p</sub>, so the constant-volume line is steeper.

quiz.q: A reversible Carnot cycle on a T-s diagram has isotherms at 400 K and 300 K and entropy limits 1 kJ/K and 2 kJ/K. Find the net work.
quiz.a: Area = (400 − 300) × (2 − 1) = 100 kJ. The net work is 100 kJ.

quiz.q: A process is irreversible between states 1 and 2. Can you find ΔS by integrating δQ/T along the real path? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Along the real irreversible path, ∫δQ/T is less than ΔS. Use a reversible path between the same two states to compute ΔS.

quiz.q: Which area on a T-s diagram gives heat for a reversible process?
quiz.a: The signed area under the path from state 1 to state 2, Q<sub>rev</sub> = ∫T dS.

beyond: Not for the exam. Entropy also appears in information theory as Shannon entropy and in computing as a limit on erasing bits. In energy studies, entropy generation is the root of exergy destruction, so it decides where a power plant loses available work. Statistical mechanics explains it as S = k<sub>B</sub> ln W, a count of microscopic arrangements. Search next: entropy generation, exergy, Shannon entropy, statistical entropy.
